694.title: bhakti — the Narada Bhakti Sutras opening
694.hook: four teachers are asked what bhakti looks like, and the book lets every one of them answer
694.carry: bhakti — the Narada Bhakti Sutras opening
694.howItsDone: In many Vaishnava homes and temples, devotion takes all four shapes the sutras name: daily puja, retelling and singing the stories of Krishna or Rama, quiet remembrance, and offering one's work to God. Groups often study a few sutras at a time with a teacher's commentary.

segments.voice: Yesterday: bhakti, and the opening of the Narada Bhakti Sutras. Now, then, we will explain bhakti; and the definition, supreme love. Which love did you catch yourself meaning? Day six hundred ninety-four.

Ask four people who love someone how you can tell, and you'll get four answers. One says: they show up. One says: they can't stop talking about them. One says: they're just happy. And one says: watch what happens when they're apart. The Narada Bhakti Sutras do something like that. A little way into the book, having defined bhakti as supreme love, they stop and ask: but what are its marks? And instead of one answer, they let four teachers speak.
screen: `HOW CAN YOU TELL SOMEONE LOVES?` → `FOUR PEOPLE, FOUR ANSWERS.` → `THE SUTRAS ASK THE SAME.`

segments.voice: Sutra fifteen sets it up: now its marks are described, according to different views. First, Vyasa, the son of Parashara, the sage tradition credits with the Mahabharata. For him, bhakti is fondness for worship: the lamp, the flowers, the offering. Second, Garga. For him, it's fondness for talk about the Lord: the stories, told and retold. Third, Shandilya. For him, it's delight in the Self that nothing gets in the way of. Three teachers, three marks, and the text doesn't call any of them wrong. Then sutra nineteen gives Narada's own view. Bhakti is offering every action to the Lord, and feeling the deepest anguish on forgetting him. The word there is vyakulata: being thrown into turmoil, unsettled, like someone who's lost a child in a crowd. It's a striking definition. Love is measured not only by what you do, but by how much it hurts to forget. Then the sutras give an example: it is like the cowherd women of Vraja, the gopis, who loved Krishna. And they head off a misreading. Even the gopis, the text says, did not forget his greatness. Love without that, it says, would be like the love of a secret lover, who takes no joy in the beloved's joy. So here, at its opening, a short book on devotion makes room for several teachers before it speaks for itself. Four marks, then: the lamp and flowers, the stories, the quiet joy, and the ache. The book keeps all four.
screen: `VYASA: FONDNESS FOR WORSHIP.` · `GARGA: LOVE OF THE STORIES.` · `SHANDILYA: DELIGHT IN THE SELF.` · `NARADA: ANGUISH ON FORGETTING.` · then, large: `LIKE THE GOPIS OF VRAJA.`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably and let the breath settle. Bring back what you love most, the one from yesterday. Now try each teacher's mark, lightly. Is there something you do for it, a small act of care? Is there a story about it you love to tell? Is there a plain gladness, just that it exists? And if it slipped out of your mind for a whole day, would you feel the gap? No answer is the right one. Let them come, and then just breathe. The bell holds the time.
Bhakti. Devotion. Vyasa sees it in worship, Garga in the stories, Shandilya in delight, and Narada in the ache of forgetting.
Your line: bhakti — the Narada Bhakti Sutras opening. Today, offer one ordinary action, a meal, a reply, a walk, to what you love, and notice if you forget. Day six hundred ninety-four.

695.title: jnana — Shankara's *Atmabodha*
695.hook: a short Sanskrit poem says action can't remove ignorance, any more than sweeping can remove the dark
695.howItsDone: In Advaita Vedanta circles, the Atmabodha is often among the first texts a student reads with a teacher, verse by verse, alongside listening, reflection and meditation on the teaching. Many Hindus combine study like this with work done as service and with devotion.

segments.voice: Yesterday: bhakti, and four teachers in the Narada Bhakti Sutras: worship, the stories, delight, and Narada's own, the ache of forgetting. Did you offer one ordinary action? Day six hundred ninety-five.

Walk into a dark room. You could sweep it. You could scrub the floor, rearrange the furniture, work there all night. None of it removes the dark. One thing does, and it takes no effort at all: the light. That picture sits near the beginning of a short Sanskrit poem called the Atmabodha, knowledge of the Self, which tradition gives to Shankara. Today the third strand of this lineage track: after karma, the path of action, and bhakti, the path of love, jnana, the path of knowing.
screen: `A DARK ROOM.` → `SWEEPING WON'T HELP.` → `THE THIRD STRAND: JNANA.`

segments.voice: The Atmabodha is short, under seventy verses, a kind of pocket handbook of Advaita Vedanta, the teaching that the Self and Brahman are not two. Tradition credits it to Shankara; some scholars question whether he wrote it, and it's often studied as a beginner's text. The first verse says who it's for: people whose faults have been worn down by discipline, who are calm, free of craving, and long for freedom. So it starts where the karma days left off: a life of work has prepared the mind. Then the second verse makes its claim. Just as fire is what actually cooks the food, the poem says, knowledge, not any other practice, is what directly brings liberation. Verse three gives the reason. Action isn't opposed to ignorance, so action can't destroy it. Knowledge is opposed to it, the way light is opposed to darkness. And verse four: because of ignorance, the Self seems limited; when ignorance goes, the Self shines on its own, like the sun when the clouds pass. The word jnana means knowing, from the root jna, to know. But it doesn't mean collecting facts. It's closer to the moment you see that the thing you feared was never there. Here the schools of Vedanta take different roads. Shankara's school holds that knowledge alone liberates, and that action and devotion ready the mind for it. Teachers in Ramanuja's tradition hold that devotion to the Lord, supported by knowledge, is the way. Both are living Hindu paths, and many Hindus walk a little of all three.
screen: `FOR THE CALM WHO LONG TO BE FREE.` · `FIRE COOKS; KNOWLEDGE FREES.` · `LIGHT, NOT SWEEPING, ENDS THE DARK.` · `THE SUN BEHIND THE CLOUDS.` · then, large: `JNANA: KNOWING.`

segments.voice: Sit still and let the breath be easy. Notice something simple: you're aware. Sounds come and go, and you're aware of them. Thoughts come and go, and you're aware of them. Feelings in the body come and go. Don't chase any of them. Just rest as the one who notices, the way the sky stays while the clouds cross it. If you drift, that's fine; noticing the drift is the practice too. The bell holds the time.
Jnana. Knowing, from the root to know. In the Atmabodha, the light that ends the dark of ignorance.
Your line: jnana — Shankara's Atmabodha. Today, when a worry looms, ask once: is this a snake, or just a shadow I haven't put the light on? Day six hundred ninety-five.

original.note: Sanskrit jñāna, knowing, from the root jñā, to know; the title Ātmabodha (आत्मबोध) means awakening to the Self.

trapdoor: what you thought: jnana means book learning.
what it means: it's knowing the Self directly, the light that ends ignorance.
what a scholar hears: Atmabodha 2–4 argue knowledge, not action, is opposed to avidya; Shankara's authorship is traditional and debated.

sources.ref: Ramanuja's view of bhakti and knowledge (Vishishtadvaita), in general

696.title: Year two close
696.hook: three hundred sixty-five sessions: seven Upanishads, the Yoga Sutras, the whole Ramayana, a year of festivals, and three paths
696.tomorrow: Adi Parva: the snake sacrifice frame
696.howItsDone: Many Hindus mark the end of a course of study, or the completion of a text, with a closing recitation, a peace chant, and an offering of thanks to the teacher. Some families sponsor a reading or feed guests when a long recitation is finished.

segments.voice: Yesterday: jnana, and Shankara's Atmabodha. Sweeping won't clear a dark room; only the light does. Was there a shadow you put the light on? Today, the last day of year two. Day six hundred ninety-six.

Three hundred sixty-five sessions ago, year two opened with a promise: the texts underneath. Not the stories people tell about Hinduism, but the old pages the stories rest on. Since then you've sat with a father telling his son, that you are. You've read a sage defining yoga in four Sanskrit words. You've walked the whole Ramayana, from a bird's cry to the earth opening. You've kept a year of festivals. Today we stand at the top and look back down the slope.
screen: `THE TEXTS UNDERNEATH.` → `THREE HUNDRED SIXTY-FIVE SESSIONS.` → `LOOK BACK DOWN THE SLOPE.`

segments.voice: Four blocks. First, the seven big Upanishads: the Chandogya, the Brihadaranyaka, the Taittiriya, the Aitareya, the Prashna, the Mundaka and the Shvetashvatara. Uddalaka and the salt in the water, and his line to Shvetaketu, tat tvam asi, that you are. Gargi asking her questions like arrows. The two kinds of knowledge. Second, the Yoga Sutras of Patanjali, in four parts, opening with atha, now, and then the definition: yoga is the stilling of the turnings of the mind. Third, Valmiki's Ramayana, seven books in a hundred and eighty sessions: a bow broken, sandals on a throne, a leap across the sea, a homecoming, and a later book whose ending the tradition still argues over with love. Fourth, the festival year, from Janmashtami's midnight to Holi's colors, and then the three strands of the lineage track. Karma, with the Isha asking the mind to remember what was done. Bhakti, with Narada's supreme love and the ache of forgetting. Jnana, with Shankara's light in the dark room. Why call it the summit of the texts? Because almost everything that comes next stands on these pages. Later teachers quote the Upanishads constantly. Yoga teachers still start from Patanjali's sutras. Poets in many languages retold Valmiki. Hindus don't all read these texts the same way, and the schools you met this week read them differently. But they read the same roots. Tomorrow, year three begins with the longest poem of all, the Mahabharata, and it opens not with a battle but with a king and a sacrifice of snakes.
screen: `SEVEN UPANISHADS: THAT YOU ARE.` · `PATANJALI: STILLING THE MIND.` · `VALMIKI: SEVEN BOOKS.` · `FESTIVALS, AND THREE PATHS.` · then, large: `YOU'VE READ THE ROOTS.`

segments.voice: Sit as if at the top of a hill, the whole year below you. Let one line from year two rise on its own: that you are, or the stilling of the mind, or remember what was done, or anything else that stayed. Don't choose; wait for it. When it comes, hold it in the breath, in on the first half, out on the second. Then let it rest, and just look out over the year. The bell holds the time.
The summit of the texts. Seven Upanishads, the Yoga Sutras, the Ramayana, the festival year, and three paths, read at the source.
screen: `THE SUMMIT OF THE TEXTS — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: you've read the roots. Today, tell one person one thing from year two that surprised you. Day six hundred ninety-six, and year two is done.

screen: `DAY 696 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: ADI PARVA: THE SNAKE SACRIFICE FRAME.`
